title: Best Before date: Yes, maps are perishable too
html:
On more than one occasion, I have been deployed to emergencies where people used an outdated map*, were confused when a new version of a map would be produced, or complained about the style of map without realizing they were not the target audience. And, yes, one occasion included threats of cutting funding because a senior official in HQ did not understand that they were looking at a field-focused tactical map rather than an advocacy map intended for their press conference. With experiences like these over the years I started to ask: should maps have a best before date and target audience stamped on them? Are they not perishable just like the groceries we buy?

We know that the humanitarian sector likes to make maps. So. Many. Maps. Sometimes those maps are valid for 24 hours and are intended to support a very specific tactical decision (think: urban search and rescue operations). Sometimes they are flashy maps for donor meetings or media interviews (think: awareness and fundraising). Yet, such details are not always clear to the consumer leaving them occasionally confused. Is this map still valid? Should I make a decision with this map or should I check for another version? When will the next version come out? Is this map intended for me?

This past winter, Anna Prince conducted a small investigation into map metadata with me. We wanted to know if such metadata was being included on maps in 2021. Some numbers from our findings:

  • 41 maps were analyzed from more than 20 organizations or entities (e.g. clusters) across 17 countries.
  • 0 maps included ‘best by’ or ‘next version date’
  • Note: MapAction and European Commission did provide a link to find the latest version
  • 0 maps included details about the intended audience (e.g. field vs HQ)
  • 0 maps included details about the product’s intended purpose (e.g. tactical vs advocacy)

Adding a couple pieces of noticeable metadata would greatly improve and influence how people interact with our maps. If we put the user at the centre of our work, does adjusting our metadata not seem like an easy way to improve their experience?

Below are a couple simple mockups of how such metadata could be included. (Actual implementation would depend on an organization’s design standards and requirements.) 

Although we did not find any examples of such metadata in use, I have to assume that someone has done so in a humanitarian operation somewhere. If you know of such efforts, please let me know by commenting below.

Andrej

* My use of ‘map’ includes both maps and infographics
teaser: Maps are perishable too: a case for best-before dates and target audiences on maps and infographics, after a small study found no examples in use.
seo_description: Why humanitarian maps may need a best-before date and a stated audience, with a small investigation by Anna Prince into map metadata.
